To reset your password:

1. Go to the sign-in page and select **“Forgot password?”**
2. Enter the email address associated with your account.
3. Check your **Inbox**, **Spam/Junk**, **Promotions**, and **Trash** folders.
4. Search for messages containing **“password reset”** or the service’s name.
5. Wait a few minutes, then request a new link. Use the **most recent** reset email, since older links may expire.
6. Confirm you entered the correct email address and check whether your mailbox is full or blocking automated messages.
7. If you still don’t receive it, contact the service’s support team through its official website.

For security, don’t share your password or reset code with anyone, and only use links from the official service domain.

Usually, you can download it from your account’s **Billing** or **Invoices** section:

1. Open **Settings** or **Account**
2. Select **Billing / Payments**
3. Find last month’s invoice
4. Click **Download**, **View invoice**, or the PDF icon

I can give exact steps if you tell me which service or website you’re using.

Assuming you mean **ChatGPT**:

| | **Pro** | **Team** *(now often called Business)* |
|---|---|---|
| **Best for** | Individual power users | Organizations and collaborative teams |
| **Users** | One person | Multiple users in a shared workspace |
| **Main benefit** | Much higher usage limits and access to advanced/pro models and features | Team workspace, centralized billing, member/admin controls, and collaboration tools |
| **Data usage** | Subject to individual-plan data settings | Business data is generally not used to train models by default |
| **Administration** | No organization-level administration | Admin console, user management, and security controls |
| **Billing** | Individual subscription | Per-user organizational billing, typically with a seat minimum |

Choose **Pro** if you work alone and mainly need maximum capacity. Choose **Team/Business** if you need shared workspaces, multiple seats, administrative controls, or stronger organizational data handling. Pricing and exact model limits can change, so the current pricing page is the definitive source.

To cancel before your free trial becomes paid:

1. **Open the service’s account or subscription settings.**
2. Select **Manage subscription**, **Billing**, or **Membership**.
3. Choose **Cancel trial** or **Cancel subscription**, then confirm.
4. Look for a **cancellation confirmation email** or verify the subscription shows an end date/no renewal.

If you subscribed through a third party:

- **iPhone/iPad:** Settings → your name → **Subscriptions** → select the service → **Cancel Subscription**.
- **Android/Google Play:** Play Store → profile icon → **Payments & subscriptions** → **Subscriptions** → select the service → **Cancel**.
- **PayPal:** Settings → Payments → **Automatic Payments** → select the merchant → cancel.

Cancel before the trial’s stated renewal time—preferably at least 24 hours early. Deleting the app usually does **not** cancel the trial.

Sorry about the unexpected charge. A $49 charge on a $29 plan can sometimes be caused by:

- Taxes or regional fees
- A prorated charge after changing plans or billing dates
- An add-on, extra seat, or usage charge
- A failed/duplicate payment attempt or a charge from a different subscription

Please check the invoice/receipt in your billing settings—the line items should show exactly what made up the $49 total. If you share the invoice date and the listed line items (please redact payment details), I can help interpret it.

Absolutely — please share the invoice details (you can redact personal/payment information), especially:

- Previous plan and price
- New plan and price
- Billing-cycle start/end dates
- Upgrade date
- Any credits, taxes, or discounts shown
- The exact prorated line items and amounts

Typically, a mid-cycle upgrade is calculated as:

> **Credit for unused time on the old plan**  
> **+ charge for the remaining time on the new plan**  
> **= net prorated amount due**

For example, if you move from a $30/month plan to a $60/month plan halfway through a 30-day cycle:

- Unused half of old plan: **–$15 credit**
- Remaining half of new plan: **+$30 charge**
- Net upgrade charge: **$15** (plus any applicable tax)

Paste the line items or upload the invoice text, and I’ll walk through the exact calculation.

I’m sorry about that. I can help verify the duplicate charge and arrange for the extra payment to be refunded.

Please provide:
- The invoice number
- The dates and amounts of both charges
- The last 4 digits of the card used (do not send the full card number)
- Any transaction/reference IDs shown on your statement, if available

If one of the charges is still marked **pending**, it may be a temporary authorization that drops off automatically rather than a completed payment.

I’m sorry this happened. I don’t have access to your account or billing system to issue a refund or confirm cancellation directly.

Please contact the service’s billing/support team with:

- The account email or customer ID  
- The date you originally cancelled  
- The three charge dates and amounts  
- A request for written confirmation that the subscription is cancelled and that all post-cancellation charges are refunded  

You can send:

> I cancelled my subscription on [date], but I was charged on [dates] for [amounts]. Please immediately confirm the subscription is cancelled, refund all charges made after my cancellation date, and provide written confirmation of both.

Include any cancellation confirmation email or screenshot if you have it. If they don’t resolve it promptly, contact your card issuer/bank to dispute the post-cancellation charges, keeping copies of your cancellation evidence and support correspondence.

This usually means the CSV exports timestamps in **UTC**, while the dashboard displays them in your configured or browser-local timezone. A 5-hour difference commonly corresponds to **Eastern Standard Time (UTC−5)**; during daylight saving time, it may be 4 hours.

Try the following:

1. Check the dashboard’s **timezone setting** under account, profile, workspace, or report settings.
2. Look for a **timezone/export timezone** option when exporting.
3. Confirm whether the CSV column header or documentation labels the timestamps as UTC.
4. If UTC export is expected, convert the column in Excel/Sheets to your local timezone. Avoid simply subtracting five hours year-round because daylight saving time can change the offset.

If you share the reporting product, your configured timezone, and an example dashboard/CSV timestamp, I can give exact steps or a conversion formula.

No, that’s generally not expected. After a successful bulk delete, the items should disappear from the list immediately—either through a local UI update or by refetching/invalidating the list data.

If they disappear only after a refresh, the delete is succeeding but the client-side list state/cache isn’t being updated.

Sorry you’re dealing with this. A green status page may not reflect account- or endpoint-specific delivery issues.

Please check the webhook delivery dashboard/history:

- **No delivery attempts:** confirm the endpoint is enabled, subscribed to the expected events, in the correct environment (test vs. production), and hasn’t been automatically disabled.
- **Attempts show 2xx:** inspect CDN/load-balancer/WAF logs and verify the configured URL. The request may be accepted upstream but not reach your application.
- **Attempts show timeouts or non-2xx:** check DNS, TLS certificate/chain, redirects, IP allowlists, authentication, and whether the endpoint responds within the required timeout.
- Send a **test delivery** if available, or POST a harmless sample directly to the endpoint to isolate provider delivery from your infrastructure.

To investigate further, share:

1. The platform/product sending the webhooks  
2. Approximate first failure time and timezone (for example, September 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC)  
3. Endpoint ID or hostname—redact secrets and query tokens  
4. A delivery/event ID and the delivery status shown in the dashboard  
5. Whether configuration, DNS, certificates, firewall/WAF rules, or deployments changed recently  

Do not post the webhook signing secret.

That sounds like a bug in the invite flow: the UI accepts the address and reports success, but the backend or email service may be mishandling the `+` character.

**Workaround:** Invite the teammate using the base address (for example, `me@gmail.com`) or another address without a `+` alias. If a pending invite exists, cancel/remove it before retrying.

Also check spam, though the misleading “sent” status suggests a delivery/validation issue. The system should either send to the full alias address unchanged or show an explicit error—not mark it as sent.

That combination is concerning and could mean someone accessed your account—but it isn’t proof. Login locations can be inaccurate because of VPNs, mobile networks, or IP-location errors. Being logged out everywhere can happen after a password change, a security reset, or the service detecting suspicious activity.

**Treat it as a possible compromise for now:**

1. **Open the service’s official app or type its website address yourself.** Don’t use links or phone numbers in the alert—it could be phishing.
2. **If you can sign in, change your password** to a new, unique one. Review recent logins, sign out unfamiliar devices—or all sessions—and remove unknown connected apps.
3. **Check your recovery email, phone number, and two-factor settings** for changes. Enable two-factor authentication or a passkey if available.
4. **Secure the email account linked to it**, especially if you reused the same password. Your email can be used to reset other accounts.
5. **If you can’t sign in, use the official account-recovery process.** Unexpected changes to your password or recovery details make an account takeover more likely.

Don’t share passwords, verification codes, or recovery codes with anyone claiming to help.

Which service is this, and can you still sign in through its official app or website?

That’s urgent. I can help you find the right recovery path, but I can’t access the account or reverse the change myself.

**Which service is the admin account for, and is anyone still signed in or able to access it through another admin account?** Don’t share passwords, recovery codes, or verification links here.

In the meantime:
- **Check the original recovery inbox** for an email-change notification. Some services offer a time-limited reversal option. Verify the sender and link destination before using it; if unsure, navigate directly to the service’s official support site.
- **Preserve any existing authorized session—don’t sign out yet.** It may let you restore recovery settings or contact authenticated support.
- **Start the official compromised-account recovery process immediately.** If another authorized admin is available, ask them to check whether they can restore access.
- **Secure the original recovery mailbox** if it may also be compromised: change its password, enable MFA, and check for unfamiliar forwarding rules.

If the change wasn’t authorized, treat this as a potential account takeover and notify your security/IT team. Save the notification and approximate time of the change for the recovery request.

Treat the key as compromised until you can explain the traffic. An unfamiliar IP isn’t proof of misuse—it could be a proxy, NAT gateway, or vendor—but don’t wait for certainty to contain it.

## 1. Contain and rotate

- **If suspicious requests are ongoing, revoke or disable the old key now**, even if that causes a temporary outage.
- If you need to preserve availability and there’s no sign of active harm:
  1. Create a replacement key with the **minimum permissions and scope** needed.
  2. Put it in your secrets manager or deployment configuration—not source code.
  3. Update every consumer: applications, background workers, scheduled jobs, CI/CD, and integrations.
  4. Redeploy or restart anything that caches credentials.
  5. Verify the replacement works, then **revoke the old key promptly**. Keep the overlap as short as possible.

Creating a new key usually does **not** invalidate the old one. Confirm revocation in the provider’s dashboard or API, and watch for authentication failures from any consumers you missed.

If available, temporarily restrict access by IP, reduce permissions, or lower usage limits. These are additional containment measures, not substitutes for revocation.

## 2. Preserve evidence and check for damage

Export relevant logs before they expire, but don’t delay revocation to do so. Preserve key IDs, request IDs, timestamps and time zones, source IPs, endpoints, status codes, and usage/billing records. Avoid copying raw secrets into incident notes.

Review from the **earliest plausible exposure**, not just the first suspicious request:

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Authentication | Did those requests actually use this key, and did authentication succeed? |
| Usage and costs | Spikes in request volume, expensive operations, quota exhaustion, or new charges |
| Data access | Unusual reads, searches, downloads, exports, or access to sensitive records |
| Changes | Created, modified, or deleted resources; altered settings or permissions |
| Persistent access | New keys, tokens, users, webhooks, integrations, or scheduled jobs |
| Downstream exposure | Other credentials or systems accessible using this key |

Compare suspicious activity with known deployments and legitimate egress IPs. **Successful responses show that an operation succeeded, but don’t necessarily reveal exactly what data was returned.** Missing logs also don’t prove nothing happened.

If the key had access to other secrets, rotate those too. Don’t rotate unrelated credentials blindly unless there’s evidence that the broader environment was compromised.

## 3. Find and close the leak

Check repositories and commit history, CI logs, build artifacts, application logs, public frontend bundles, container images, tickets/chat, and developer machines.

Removing a key from the current file or rewriting repository history does **not** make it safe again—revocation is essential. If it was embedded in browser or mobile code, move privileged API calls to a backend; those clients cannot keep a shared secret confidential.

## 4. Recover and monitor

- Undo unauthorized changes after recording evidence.
- Enable usage alerts, tighter scopes, and separate keys per service/environment.
- Contact the provider’s security/support team for additional audit records and billing review.
- If customer or regulated data may have been accessed, involve your security/privacy team promptly to assess notification obligations.

**Which provider is the key for, and is suspicious traffic still happening?** I can give exact rotation steps and log queries. Don’t paste the key itself.

I can help you find the recovery process, but I can’t access your account or disable two-factor authentication. Which service is the account with?

To regain access today, check for:
- **Backup or recovery codes** saved when you enabled 2FA.
- **Another verification method** offered on the sign-in screen, such as a security key, recovery email, or another device.
- **A device where you’re still signed in**—don’t sign out. You may be able to update your security settings there, though verification may still be required.
- **Your mobile carrier**, if the codes arrive by SMS; it may be able to restore your number on a replacement SIM.

If none work, use the service’s official account-recovery process. Recovery may not be immediate. Don’t share passwords or verification codes here or with anyone offering to bypass 2FA.
Which dashboard or product are you referring to? The **“last active”** timestamp’s timezone varies by platform—often it uses your account, organization, browser, or UTC timezone.

Treat this as an observability and containment incident before trying to infer a bad field.

### Immediate containment
- Add an end-to-end reconciliation check: `source IDs − destination IDs`, grouped by batch/run.
- Persist dropped/failed records to a dead-letter queue rather than skipping them.
- Retry only with idempotent writes and stable record IDs.
- If possible, replay the last week’s missing IDs after validating downstream side effects.

### Instrument each stage
For every record, emit a structured event containing:

- `run_id`, `batch_id`, stable `record_id`
- source read timestamp/version
- stage entered/exited and outcome
- validation/filter decision and reason
- serialization payload size and schema version
- destination status/error code
- retry count, worker/host, partition/shard
- queue lag and processing duration

Avoid logging sensitive payloads; log hashes or relevant metadata instead.

### Likely intermittent causes
Prioritize checking:

1. Unhandled partial batch failures or incorrect success accounting  
2. Timeouts/cancellations where the batch advances its checkpoint anyway  
3. Pagination/cursor bugs, especially with changing source data  
4. Concurrent updates or non-stable ordering during pagination  
5. Rate limits, transient destination errors, or connection pool exhaustion  
6. Worker termination after dequeue but before commit  
7. Partition-specific failures or poison records affecting adjacent records  
8. Filters/default branches that silently return success  
9. Payload-size or encoding limits  
10. Clock/window boundary issues and late-arriving records

### Fast diagnostic
Compare included vs. missing records across:

- worker, partition, batch size, and position within batch
- hour/time window and deployment version
- retry count, latency, and payload size
- source update frequency/version
- destination response code

A roughly 2% random-looking loss often becomes obvious when grouped by worker, partition, or batch position.

Most importantly, verify checkpoint semantics: the source checkpoint should advance only after every record in the covered range is durably written or durably queued for retry.

If you mean **ChatGPT**, the main difference is: **Pro is for one person who needs higher usage; Team is for an organization that needs a shared, managed workspace.** Team has since been renamed **ChatGPT Business**.

| | **Pro** | **Team / Business** |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Heavy individual use | Multiple people working together |
| Main benefit | Higher individual usage limits and access to advanced capabilities | Business workspace, collaboration, and administration |
| Billing | Individual subscription | Per-user billing, typically with a minimum of two users |
| Administration | Personal account settings | Centralized billing and member management |
| Collaboration | Primarily individual use | Shared workspace and workspace GPTs |
| Training privacy | You can opt out of having conversations used for model training | Workspace data isn’t used for model training by default |

**Which should you choose?**
- **Choose Pro** if you work alone and primarily want more access to demanding AI features.
- **Choose Business** if you need accounts for colleagues, company administration, and business-data protections.

Business isn’t simply “Pro for every employee”—its usage limits and included capabilities can differ. Exact pricing, model access, and limits change, so check the current plan comparison before purchasing.
